claim: Thymic macrophages express CD64, F4/80, and MerTK.
source: To unambiguously and comprehensively identify macrophages in the thymus, we evaluated several of the prototypical macrophage markers – MerTK, CD64, and F4/80 (Gautier et al., 2012) – a population that was stained with all three markers (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1A showing co-expression of these markers, and by the citation to Gautier et al., 2012 establishing these as prototypical macrophage markers.

claim: CD64+F4/80+MerTK+CD11bloFSChi cells have typical macrophage morphology with abundant cytoplasm.
source: The CD64+F4/80+MerTK+CD11bloFSChi cells had typical macrophage morphology with abundant cytoplasm (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by cytospin images in Figure 1C showing morphological characteristics.

claim: Thymic macrophages do not express lineage markers characteristic of T cells (CD3ε), B cells (CD19), eosinophils (Siglec F), NK cells (NK1.1), neutrophils (Gr1), or plasmacytoid dendritic cells (Siglec H).
source: These cells did not express lineage markers characteristic of T cells (CD3ε), B cells (CD19), eosinophils (Siglec F), NK cells (NK1.1), neutrophils (Gr1), or plasmacytoid dendritic cells (Siglec H) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1D showing absence of these markers.

claim: Thymic macrophages express phagocytic receptors TIM4, CD51, and Axl.
source: However, they expressed phagocytic receptors such as TIM4, CD51, and Axl (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1E showing expression of these receptors.

claim: MerTK+ cells cannot be labeled by intravenously injected CD45 antibody, proving they reside in the parenchyma of the organs and not in the blood vessels.
source: Importantly, MerTK+ cells could not be labeled by intravenously injected CD45 antibody (Figure 1F), proving that they reside in the parenchyma of the organs and not in the blood vessels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1F showing lack of labeling with intravenously injected antibody.

claim: Thymic macrophages are approximately 0.1% of all cells in the thymus of young adult mice and number approximately 4×10^5 on average per mouse.
source: Thymic macrophages were ~0.1% of all the cells in the thymus of young adult mice and numbered ~4×105 on average per mouse (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by quantitative flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: There is a significant decline in thymic macrophage numbers with age between 4 and 11 weeks, consistent with the beginning of thymic involution.
source: Still, there was a significant decline in their numbers with age, consistent with the beginning of thymic involution (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1H showing age-dependent changes.

claim: Core signature macrophage genes are enriched in thymic macrophages but not in Sirpa+ or Xcr1+ thymic cDCs.
source: We first examined the expression of the core signature macrophage genes (Gautier et al., 2012) and found that they were enriched in thymic macrophages but not in Sirpa+ or Xcr1+ thymic cDCs (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2A and citation to Gautier et al., 2012 defining core macrophage genes.

claim: cDC core signature genes are abundantly expressed in both thymic cDC subsets but not in thymic macrophages.
source: On the contrary, cDC core signature genes were abundantly expressed in both thymic cDC subsets but not in thymic macrophages.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data comparing gene expression between cell types.

claim: Thymic macrophages are most closely related to splenic red pulp macrophages and Kupffer cells based on gene expression profile.
source: Principal component analysis revealed that thymic macrophages were most closely related to splenic red pulp macrophages and Kupffer cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by principal component analysis of RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 44 genes constitute the transcriptional signature of thymic macrophages based on high expression (>500), >5-fold higher expression than average in nine non-thymic macrophage populations, and higher expression than any non-thymic macrophage sample.
source: We set three criteria: (1) high expression in thymic macrophages (>500); (2) >fivefold higher expression than the average value in the nine populations of non-thymic macrophages; (3) expression in thymic macrophages is higher than any non-thymic macrophage samples. A total of 44 genes met these criteria, and we consider them to constitute the transcriptional signature of thymic macrophages (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 25 transcription factors are highly expressed in thymic macrophages (>250) and are at least twofold higher compared to non-thymic macrophages.
source: A total of 25 TFs were highly expressed in thymic macrophages (>250) and were at least twofold higher as compared to the non-thymic macrophages (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by transcription factor expression analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: Spic is highly expressed in thymic macrophages.
source: Spic, which has well-documented roles in the development of red pulp macrophages in the spleen and bone marrow macrophages (Kohyama et al., 2009; Haldar et al., 2014), was also highly expressed in thymic macrophages, further strengthening the argument for the similarity between thymus, spleen, and liver macrophages.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data and citations to Kohyama et al., 2009 and Haldar et al., 2014 documenting Spic's role in other macrophage populations.

claim: All SpicGFP+ cells in the thymus are macrophages.
source: To confirm the expression of Spic in thymic macrophages, we analyzed the thymus of SpicGFP mice (Haldar et al., 2014). We found that all SpicGFP+ cells were macrophages (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), making them the most specific thymic macrophage reporter strain compared with Lyz2GFP, MAFIA (Csf1rGFP), Cd11cYFP, and Cx3cr1GFP mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis in SpicGFP reporter mice shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and comparison with other reporter strains in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only approximately 80% of thymic macrophages are SpicGFP+, suggesting heterogeneity within the cells.
source: However, only ~80% of thymic macrophages were SpicGFP+ suggesting heterogeneity within the cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Five of the 10 most highly enriched GO pathways in thymic macrophages concern antigen presentation of both exogenous and endogenous antigens.
source: Notably, 5 of the 10 most highly enriched GO pathways concerned antigen presentation of both exogenous and endogenous antigens.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of highly expressed genes.

claim: Two highly enriched GO pathways in thymic macrophages are involved in lysosomal biogenesis and functions.
source: Two other highly enriched GO pathways were involved in lysosomal biogenesis and functions, highlighting the high capacity of these cells to degrade phagocytosed material.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Thymic macrophages can induce proliferation in approximately 30% of OT2 cells when pulsed with chicken ovalbumin.
source: Surprisingly, thymic macrophages induced proliferation in a considerable proportion (~30%) of OT2 cells as calculated by FlowJo's Proliferation Modeling module.
evidence: Supported by in vitro antigen presentation assay data analyzed with FlowJo's Proliferation Modeling module.

claim: Thymic macrophages are able antigen-presenting cells, although not as good as DCs.
source: Thus, thymic macrophages are able antigen-presenting cells, although not as good as DCs.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of OT2 cell proliferation induced by thymic macrophages versus thymic DCs in the antigen presentation assay.

claim: Thymic macrophages are avid phagocytes in vitro.
source: Thymic macrophages were avid phagocytes, and we could record many instances of efferocytosis at this time point (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: On average, approximately 85% of all TUNEL+ cells are within 5 µm of MerTK+ cells in the thymus.
source: On average, ~85% of all TUNEL+ cells were within 5 µm of MerTK+ cells, confirming that thymic macrophages are the dominant phagocytic population in the thymus (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent co-localization analysis quantified in Figure 3G.

claim: Thymic macrophages are the dominant phagocytic population in the thymus.
source: On average, ~85% of all TUNEL+ cells were within 5 µm of MerTK+ cells, confirming that thymic macrophages are the dominant phagocytic population in the thymus (Figure 3G).
evidence: Inferred from the high degree of co-localization between TUNEL+ apoptotic cells and MerTK+ macrophages.

claim: Thymic macrophages consist of two populations distinguished by the expression of Timd4 and Cx3cr1.
source: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-Seq) showed that the macrophages in the adult thymus are composed of two populations distinguished by the expression of Timd4 and Cx3cr1.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA sequencing analysis identifying distinct populations.

claim: Timd4+ thymic macrophages are located in the cortex.
source: Remarkably, Timd4+ cells were located in the cortex, while Cx3cr1+ macrophages were restricted to the medulla and the cortico-medullary junction.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent localization studies.

claim: Cx3cr1+ macrophages are restricted to the medulla and the cortico-medullary junction.
source: Remarkably, Timd4+ cells were located in the cortex, while Cx3cr1+ macrophages were restricted to the medulla and the cortico-medullary junction.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent localization studies shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Timd4+ thymic macrophages are of embryonic origin.
source: Timd4+ thymic macrophages are of embryonic origin, while Cx3cr1+ macrophages are derived from adult hematopoietic stem cells.
evidence: Supported by shield chimera experiments, embryonic thymus transplantation, and genetic fate mapping experiments.

claim: Cx3cr1+ macrophages are derived from adult hematopoietic stem cells.
source: Timd4+ thymic macrophages are of embryonic origin, while Cx3cr1+ macrophages are derived from adult hematopoietic stem cells.
evidence: Supported by shield chimera experiments, embryonic thymus transplantation, and genetic fate mapping experiments.

claim: At E15.5, more than 50% of thymic macrophages are derived from yolk sac progenitors.
source: After adjusting for incomplete labeling based on the microglia, we found that at E15.5 >50% of thymic macrophages were fate mapped, i.e., from YS origin (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by Cx3cr1CreER fate mapping experiments at E9.5 analyzed at E15.5, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: GFP+ thymic macrophages derived from yolk sac progenitors decrease to approximately 11% at E19.5.
source: However, GFP+ thymic macrophages decreased to just ~11% at E19.5, suggesting that YS progenitors establish the embryonic thymic macrophage pool but are quickly replaced by subsequent wave(s) of macrophages.
evidence: Supported by fate mapping data showing temporal changes in YS-derived macrophage proportions.

claim: YS progenitors establish the embryonic thymic macrophage pool but are quickly replaced by subsequent wave(s) of macrophages.
source: However, GFP+ thymic macrophages decreased to just ~11% at E19.5, suggesting that YS progenitors establish the embryonic thymic macrophage pool but are quickly replaced by subsequent wave(s) of macrophages.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal dynamics of YS-derived macrophage proportions during embryonic development.

claim: Less than 2% of TIM4+ thymic macrophages are donor-derived in shield chimeras after 6 weeks.
source: The donor-derived monocytes in the blood were, on average, 57%, but less than 2% of TIM4+ thymic macrophages were CD45.1+ (Figure 5E and F), suggesting very limited contribution of adult circulating monocytes to the TIM4+ macrophage pool.
evidence: Supported by shield chimera experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Adult circulating monocytes have very limited contribution to the TIM4+ macrophage pool.
source: The donor-derived monocytes in the blood were, on average, 57%, but less than 2% of TIM4+ thymic macrophages were CD45.1+ (Figure 5E and F), suggesting very limited contribution of adult circulating monocytes to the TIM4+ macrophage pool.
evidence: Inferred from the low percentage of donor-derived TIM4+ macrophages despite high donor chimerism in blood monocytes.

claim: Approximately 23% of TIM4− thymic macrophages are HSC-derived in shield chimeras.
source: The percentage of HSC-derived TIM4− macrophages (on average 23%) was intermediate between the monocytes and TIM4+ macrophages, pointing out that a sizeable part of TIM4− cells was derived from adult HSCs.
evidence: Supported by shield chimera experimental data.

claim: More than 99% of thymocytes in transplanted E15.5 thymuses are derived from host HSCs after 6 weeks.
source: By that time, >99% of thymocytes in the transplanted thymus were derived from CD45.1+ host HSCs, indicating successful replacement by HSC-derived progenitors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by thymus transplantation experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: TIM4− thymic macrophages in transplanted E15.5 thymuses are derived entirely from host HSCs after 6 weeks.
source: TIM4− thymic macrophages were derived entirely from host HSCs, just like thymocytes.
evidence: Supported by thymus transplantation experimental data.

claim: The progenitors of most TIM4+ thymic macrophages are of embryonic origin.
source: The results from our transplantation experiments show that the progenitors of most TIM4+ thymic macrophages are of embryonic origin, while TIM4− cells are derived from adult monocytes.
evidence: Inferred from thymus transplantation experiments showing persistence of donor-derived TIM4+ macrophages.

claim: TIM4− thymic macrophages rely mostly on adult HSCs for their generation and replacement.
source: In contrast, TIM4− thymic macrophages rely mostly on adult HSCs for their generation and replacement.
evidence: Inferred from thymus transplantation and shield chimera experiments showing host-derived origin of TIM4− macrophages.

claim: Approximately 4% of all thymic macrophages express Ki67.
source: Staining for the proliferation marker Ki67 revealed that ~4% of all thymic macrophages expressed this marker compared to an isotype control (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Approximately 5% of thymic macrophages retain EdU label after a 21-day pulse and 21-day chase period.
source: However, ~5% of the thymic macrophages were EdU+, suggesting they divided during the labeling period.
evidence: Supported by EdU pulse-chase experimental data.

claim: Approximately 3% of thymic macrophages are in the G2/M phase of the cell cycle.
source: Although almost all thymic macrophages were in G0/G1 phase, a small population of ~3% was in the G2/M phase of the cell cycle (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis of sorted thymic macrophages shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: A small proportion (3-5%) of thymic macrophages are actively dividing under homeostatic conditions within the thymus.
source: Collectively, four independent approaches documented that a small proportion (3–5%) of thymic macrophages are actively dividing under homeostatic conditions within the thymus.
evidence: Supported by multiple independent experimental approaches: Ki67 staining, EdU pulse-chase, cell cycle analysis, and scRNA-Seq.

claim: Most dividing thymic macrophages belong to the Cx3cr1+ subset.
source: Surprisingly, most Mki67+ thymic macrophages belonged to the Cx3cr1+ subset, and only a few of the Timd4+ cells were positive (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-Seq data showing Mki67 expression patterns in Figure 6H.

claim: Ki-67 expression is significantly higher in TIM4− than in TIM4+ thymic macrophages.
source: The expression of Ki-67 was significantly higher in TIM4− than in TIM4+ thymic macrophages (Figure 6G), suggesting that the former is the more proliferative subset.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry comparison shown in Figure 6G with statistical significance.

claim: Timd4+ macrophages are primarily quiescent.
source: The majority of the dividing cells were from the adult HSC-derived Cx3cr1+ subset. Timd4+ macrophages were primarily quiescent.
evidence: Inferred from the low Ki-67 expression and low proliferation rates in TIM4+ macrophages compared to TIM4− macrophages.

claim: At E14.5, all thymic macrophages are Cx3cr1+, and only approximately 20% are also TIM4+.
source: At the earliest time point (E14.5), all thymic macrophages were Cx3cr1+, and only ~20% were also TIM4+ (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis during embryonic development shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: In the neonatal period, almost all thymic macrophages are TIM4+, and very few remain TIM4−.
source: In the neonatal period, almost all macrophages were TIM4+, and very few remained TIM4−.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis during postnatal development.

claim: There are essentially no Cx3cr1+TIM4− thymic macrophages remaining at day 7 after birth.
source: This transition is complete in the first week after birth as there were essentially no Cx3cr1+TIM4− thymic macrophages remaining at d.7 (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing temporal dynamics in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The extent of labeling of TIM4+ thymic macrophages does not change within 6 weeks after tamoxifen treatment in neonatal or adult mice.
source: The extent of labeling of TIM4+ thymic macrophages did not change within these 6 weeks, no matter whether the mice were treated with tamoxifen in the first week after birth or at 6 weeks (Figure 8B and D), suggesting an absence of a significant influx from unlabeled cells (e.g. monocytes).
evidence: Supported by fate mapping experiments in neonatal and adult mice shown in Figure 8B and D.

claim: The proportion of labeled TIM4− thymic macrophages decreases significantly 6 weeks after tamoxifen injection in neonatal and adult mice.
source: In contrast, the proportion of labeled TIM4− thymic macrophages decreased significantly 6 weeks after tamoxifen injection in neonatal and adult mice, suggesting that this population was diluted by unlabeled cells.
evidence: Supported by fate mapping experiments showing temporal changes in labeling proportions.

claim: In mice older than 8 months, TIM4− thymic macrophages account for approximately 70% of all macrophages in the thymus.
source: To further substantiate these findings, we examined older WT mice and found out that the proportions of TIM4− thymic macrophages increased with age, and in mice >8 months old, they accounted for ~70% of all macrophages in the organ (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by age-dependent analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: TIM4+ thymic macrophages reach peak numbers at an early age and then decline significantly.
source: In contrast to TIM4+ thymic macrophages that reached peak numbers at an early age and then declined significantly, TIM4− cells tended to increase their numbers in older mice (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of macrophage numbers with age shown in Figure 8F.

claim: TIM4− thymic macrophages tend to increase their numbers in older mice.
source: In contrast to TIM4+ thymic macrophages that reached peak numbers at an early age and then declined significantly, TIM4− cells tended to increase their numbers in older mice (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of macrophage numbers with age shown in Figure 8F.

claim: After birth, the numbers of TIM4+ macrophages follow the kinetics of thymus size – increase in young and decrease in old mice, and they are not replaced by other cells.
source: Thus, we conclude that, after birth, the numbers of TIM4+ macrophages follow the kinetics of the thymus size – increase in young and decrease in old mice, and they are not replaced by other cells.
evidence: Inferred from fate mapping and age-dependent quantification data.

claim: Since the first week of life, Cx3cr1+ cells are recruited to the thymus, accumulate with age, and in old mice form the predominant phagocytic population in the organ.
source: In contrast, since the first week of life, Cx3cr1+ cells are recruited to the thymus, accumulate with age, and in old mice, form the predominant phagocytic population in the organ.
evidence: Inferred from fate mapping and age-dependent quantification data showing accumulation of TIM4− (Cx3cr1+) macrophages.

claim: Thymic macrophages highly express molecules involved in antigen presentation, including MHC1 and MHC2.
source: Thymic macrophages highly express molecules involved in antigen presentation, including MHC1 and MHC2, although the latter is expressed at lower levels than in cDCs, and are functionally competent to induce T cell activation.
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data and flow cytometry showing expression of these molecules.

claim: MHC2 is expressed at lower levels in thymic macrophages than in cDCs.
source: Thymic macrophages highly express molecules involved in antigen presentation, including MHC1 and MHC2, although the latter is expressed at lower levels than in cDCs, and are functionally competent to induce T cell activation.
evidence: Supported by comparative expression analysis between thymic macrophages and cDCs.

claim: Thymic macrophages have the potential to present antigens for both negative selection and agonist selection.
source: Thus, they have the potential to present antigens for both negative selection and agonist selection.
evidence: Inferred from their expression of antigen presentation molecules and functional competence in T cell activation.

claim: Negative selection is most efficient when the cell that presents the antigen to an auto-reactive thymocyte is also the one that phagocytoses it.
source: However, recent evidence suggests that negative selection is most efficient when the cell that presents the antigen to an auto-reactive thymocyte is also the one that phagocytoses it (Kurd et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kurd et al., 2019.

claim: Thymic macrophages develop in three distinct waves: YS-derived progenitors, YS-independent embryonic progenitors, and adult HSC-derived progenitors.
source: Together with the study by Tacke et al., 2015, our work builds the following model for thymic macrophage origin: thymic macrophages develop in three distinct waves: YS-derived progenitors dominate the early stages of thymus development but are replaced before birth by a second wave of YS-independent embryonic progenitors that forms the bulk of thymic macrophages after birth and can self-maintain into adulthood. With age, there is a slow and steady influx of Timd4−Cx3cr1+ macrophage precursors that occupy the medulla and cortico-medullary junction, becoming the major phagocytic population in the thymus of older mice (>8 months).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental approaches including fate mapping, shield chimeras, and thymus transplantation, combined with citation to Tacke et al., 2015.

claim: The second wave of YS-independent macrophages is most likely the progeny of embryonic HSCs based on Flt3Cre fate mapping.
source: The second wave of YS-independent macrophages is most likely the progeny of embryonic HSCs based on Flt3Cre fate mapping that showed that >80% of thymic macrophages in adult mice are descendants of HSCs (Tacke et al., 2015), whether HSC-independent fetal liver monocytes contribute to thymic macrophages and to what extent awaits the creation of models that can specifically target this population of progenitors.
evidence: Inferred from citation to Tacke et al., 2015 showing Flt3Cre fate mapping results.

claim: Timd4+ cells are restricted to the cortex and are particularly abundant in the deeper cortex, close to the medulla.
source: Timd4+ cells are restricted to the cortex and are particularly abundant in the deeper cortex, close to the medulla.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent localization studies.

claim: Timd4+ macrophages might be specialized in efferocytosis of CD4+CD8+ (double-positive) thymocytes that die by neglect or undergo clonal deletion in the cortex.
source: Both positive and negative selection of thymocytes occur there, so we speculate that Timd4+ macrophages might be specialized in efferocytosis of CD4+CD8+ (double-positive) thymocytes that cannot interact with cortical thymic epithelial cells and die by neglect or are auto-reactive and undergo clonal deletion in the cortex (Stritesky et al., 2013).
evidence: Speculative inference based on localization of Timd4+ macrophages in the cortex where double-positive thymocyte selection occurs, with citation to Stritesky et al., 2013.

claim: Cx3cr1+ macrophages might contribute to negative selection to tissue-restricted antigens by carrying TRAs from blood and peripheral organs.
source: They might contribute to the process in several ways: (1) by carrying TRAs from blood and peripheral organs. A similar process has been described for cDC2 (SIRPα+ DCs) (Bonasio et al., 2006; Baba et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculative inference based on localization in the medulla and comparison to cDC2, with citations to Bonasio et al., 2006 and Baba et al., 2009.

claim: Cx3cr1+ macrophages might contribute to negative selection by capturing TRAs from Aire+ medullary thymic epithelial cells and presenting them to auto-reactive thymocytes.
source: (2) By capturing TRAs from Aire+ medullary thymic epithelial cells and presenting them to auto-reactive thymocytes as shown for DCs (Gallegos and Bevan, 2004; Koble and Kyewski, 2009; Vobořil et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculative inference based on comparison to DCs, with citations to Gallegos and Bevan, 2004; Koble and Kyewski, 2009; and Vobořil et al., 2020.

claim: Cx3cr1+ macrophages might contribute to negative selection by phagocytosing apoptotic TRA-specific medullary thymocytes.
source: (3) By phagocytosing apoptotic TRA-specific medullary thymocytes, a process we have observed before (Kurd et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative inference based on previous observations, with citation to Kurd et al., 2019.

claim: TGFβ1 is highly expressed in thymic macrophages, with highest expression in the Timd4+ subset.
source: Tgfb1 was highly expressed in thymic macrophages. However, its expression was the highest in the Timd4+ subset (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-Seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Cx3cr1+ thymic macrophages are the predominant producer of the growth factor PDGFα.
source: For example, Cx3cr1+ thymic macrophages are the predominant producer of the growth factor PDGFα (Figure 4G) that is required for the maintenance of adipocyte stem cells and can stimulate tissue fibrosis (Rivera-Gonzalez et al., 2016; Olson and Soriano, 2009).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-Seq differential gene expression data in Figure 4G and citations to Rivera-Gonzalez et al., 2016 and Olson and Soriano, 2009.

claim: PDGFα is required for the maintenance of adipocyte stem cells and can stimulate tissue fibrosis.
source: For example, Cx3cr1+ thymic macrophages are the predominant producer of the growth factor PDGFα (Figure 4G) that is required for the maintenance of adipocyte stem cells and can stimulate tissue fibrosis (Rivera-Gonzalez et al., 2016; Olson and Soriano, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rivera-Gonzalez et al., 2016 and Olson and Soriano, 2009.

claim: The gradual accumulation of Cx3cr1+ macrophages could increase the availability of PDGFα in the aging thymus, stimulating extracellular matrix production and differentiation of precursors into adipocytes.
source: The gradual accumulation of Cx3cr1+ macrophages could increase the availability of PDGFα in the aging thymus stimulating extracellular matrix production and differentiation of precursors into adipocytes.
evidence: Speculative inference connecting the accumulation of Cx3cr1+ macrophages with thymic involution through PDGFα.

claim: Limiting the influx of Cx3cr1+ macrophage precursors could delay thymus involution.
source: This model predicts that limiting the influx of Cx3cr1+ macrophage precursors could delay thymus involution.
evidence: Speculative prediction based on the proposed model linking Cx3cr1+ macrophage accumulation to thymic involution.

claim: Thymic macrophages express CD11c, MHC2, and SIRPα, making them partially overlap with CD11c+MHC2+ classical dendritic cells.
source: Thymic macrophages expressed CD11c, MHC2, and SIRPα making them partially overlap with CD11c+MHC2+ classical dendritic cells (cDCs), thus making problematic the unambiguous identification of thymic cDCs based only on these two markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Proper identification of cDC in the thymus requires the exclusion of macrophages based on CD64 or MerTK staining.
source: Proper identification of cDC in the thymus requires the exclusion of macrophages based on CD64 or MerTK staining.
evidence: Inferred from the overlap in marker expression between thymic macrophages and cDCs.

claim: Macrophages account for approximately 25% of cDC2 when cDCs are identified without excluding CD64 or MerTK positive cells.
source: Otherwise, the cDCs, particularly the SIRPα+ cDC2 subset, would be contaminated with macrophages that account for ~25% of cDC2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Tissue-resident macrophages are essential to protect from pathogen invasion and maintain organ homeostasis.
source: Tissue-resident macrophages are essential to protect from pathogen invasion and maintain organ homeostasis.
evidence: Represents established scientific knowledge about tissue-resident macrophages.

claim: Many tissue-resident macrophages are long-lived cells with an embryonic origin that can maintain themselves in the tissues.
source: Contrary to the long-held belief that all macrophages derive from circulating monocytes (van Furth and Cohn, 1968), multiple studies have shown that many of them are long-lived cells with an embryonic origin that can maintain themselves in the tissues (reviewed in Ginhoux and Guilliams, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Furth and Cohn, 1968 and review by Ginhoux and Guilliams, 2016.

claim: Three waves of distinct progenitors settle the tissues and contribute in various degrees to the resident macrophages in each organ.
source: Three waves of distinct progenitors settle the tissues and contribute in various degrees to the resident macrophages in each organ.
evidence: Represents established scientific knowledge about macrophage development.

claim: The first wave consists of yolk sac-derived primitive macrophages that enter all tissues and establish the earliest macrophage populations.
source: The first wave consists of the yolk sac (YS)-derived primitive macrophages that enter all tissues and establish the earliest macrophage populations (Perdiguero and Geissmann, 2016; Mass et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Perdiguero and Geissmann, 2016 and Mass et al., 2016.

claim: In all organs except for the brain and partially the epidermis, primitive macrophages are replaced by fetal monocytes.
source: In all organs, except for the brain and, partially, the epidermis, primitive macrophages are replaced by the next wave consisting of fetal monocytes (Ginhoux et al., 2010; Hoeffel et al., 2012; Hoeffel et al., 2015; Goldmann et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ginhoux et al., 2010; Hoeffel et al., 2012; Hoeffel et al., 2015; and Goldmann et al., 2016.

claim: The third wave of macrophage progenitors comes from hematopoietic stem cells-derived monocytes that contribute to various degrees to the macrophage pool in different tissues.
source: The third wave comes from hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs)-derived monocytes that contribute to various degrees to the macrophage pool in different tissues.
evidence: Represents established scientific knowledge about macrophage development.

claim: HSC-derived monocytes contribute little to microglia in the brain, Langerhans cells in the epidermis, and alveolar macrophages in the lungs but substantially to most other organs.
source: For example, these cells contribute little to the microglia in the brain, Langerhans cells in the epidermis, and alveolar macrophages in the lungs but substantially to most other organs (Hashimoto et al., 2013; Epelman et al., 2014; Sheng et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hashimoto et al., 2013; Epelman et al., 2014; Sheng et al., 2015; and Liu et al., 2019.

claim: The ability of thymic macrophages to engulf apoptotic thymocytes is well appreciated.
source: The ability of thymic macrophages to engulf apoptotic thymocytes is well appreciated, but little is known about their ontogeny, maintenance, and diversity.
evidence: Represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Little is known about the ontogeny, maintenance, and diversity of thymic macrophages.
source: The ability of thymic macrophages to engulf apoptotic thymocytes is well appreciated, but little is known about their ontogeny, maintenance, and diversity.
evidence: Represents a gap in scientific knowledge that this study addresses.

claim: There is a lack of consensus about the surface phenotype of thymic macrophages.
source: This gap in our knowledge is, partly, due to the lack of a consensus about the surface phenotype of thymic macrophages.
evidence: Represents a problem in the field that this study addresses.

claim: Various groups have used different markers to identify thymic macrophages, such as F4/80 and Mac-3 (LAMP-2), or CD4 and CD11b, or Mac-2 (galectin 3), F4/80, and ED-1 (CD68).
source: Various groups have used different markers to identify these cells, such as F4/80 and Mac-3 (LAMP-2) (Surh and Sprent, 1994), or CD4 and CD11b (Esashi et al., 2003), or Mac-2 (galectin 3), F4/80, and ED-1 (CD68) (Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Surh and Sprent, 1994; Esashi et al., 2003; and Liu et al., 2013.

claim: Most commonly, researchers employ F4/80 and CD11b to identify thymic macrophages.
